alternates.line: Wherever the restless mind wanders, gently bring it back. Again and again.

alternates.speaker: Krishna

alternates.line: Don't get carried away by good news or crushed by bad. Keep your understanding steady.
alternates.translation: One should not rejoice on getting what is pleasant nor be troubled on getting what is unpleasant. Steady in understanding and undeluded, the knower of Brahman abides in Brahman.
alternates.why: Pleasures that start and end can't hold your happiness; find the joy within.

verse.line: The mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong. Holding it feels like holding the wind.

verse.why: The mind is hard to hold, but practice and letting go train it.

prasang.title: Mastering the mind
prasang.summary: Arjuna says the mind is restless, stormy and stubborn. Krishna agrees, and says practice and letting go can train it.
prasang.lesson: The mind is hard to hold, but practice and letting go train it.

verse.meaning: Arjuna, standing on the edge of a battle he does not want, tells Krishna that the mind is restless, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. He says it is as hard to hold as the wind. Krishna agrees, and says that through practice and letting go, the mind can be trained.
verse.for_you: The restlessness you feel is the mind refusing to settle until it knows how things will turn out. Practice and letting go train it, not by forcing it to be still, but by giving it something to do. You are not failing at this.
verse.try_today: Notice one moment when the mind stops searching and simply rests.
verse.scene_line: You stand at the edge of the day, and the mind is a wind you cannot hold.
asks: How do I practice letting go when the outcome feels uncertain?
Where do I find the space to let go today?

verse.speaker: Krishna
verse.setting: Krishna on the five causes behind every action.
verse.sanskrit: अधिष्ठानं तथा कर्ता करणं च पृथग्विधम् । विविधाश्च पृथक्चेष्टा दैवं चैवात्र पञ्चमम् ॥
verse.line: Every result has five causes: the setting, the doer, the tools, the efforts, and the unseen. You're one of them.
verse.translation: The seat, the doer, the various instruments, the many kinds of effort, and fifth, providence: these are the five causes of every action.
verse.why: You are one cause among five; own your part, not the whole outcome.
verse.misuse: Not 'it wasn't my fault'. You own your part; you just aren't the only cause.

matched.label: I'm anxious about how things will turn out

prasang.title: What makes an action happen
prasang.summary: Every action has five causes: the setting, the doer, the instruments, the efforts, and providence. Seeing oneself as the only doer is a mistake.
prasang.lesson: You are one cause among five; own your part, not the whole outcome.

verse.meaning: Krishna is explaining to Arjuna why every action happens the way it does. He lists five causes behind any result: the setting, the person acting, the tools they use, the effort they put in, and something unseen. The point is that you are only one of these causes. You are the doer, but you are not the whole outcome.
verse.for_you: You are trying to hold the whole outcome in your hands while your children need you present. You are one cause among five, and the rest is not yours to manage. Your part is the effort, not the final shape of their lives.
verse.try_today: Notice one thing you did today that was your part, and let the rest go.
verse.scene_line: You stand in the middle of five causes, holding the whole outcome in your hands.
asks: How do I know my part and not the rest?
What is unseen in my children's lives?
Where does my effort end and the result begin?

verse.speaker: Krishna
verse.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on how the wise live and work.
verse.sanskrit: यदृच्छालाभसन्तुष्टो द्वन्द्वातीतो विमत्सरः । समः सिद्धावसिद्धौ च कृत्वापि न निबध्यते ॥
verse.line: Content with what comes, beyond envy, steady in success and failure, you stay free even while working.
verse.translation: Content with whatever comes unasked, beyond the pairs of opposites, free from envy, the same in success and failure, even when acting he is not bound.
verse.why: Contentment and freedom from envy let you work without being bound.

matched.label: I keep comparing myself to others

prasang.title: How the great yogis live
prasang.summary: The wise act without selfish motive, content and dependent on nothing, free from envy, steady in success and failure.
prasang.lesson: Contentment and freedom from envy let you work without being bound.

verse.meaning: Krishna is speaking to Arjuna on the battlefield, explaining how a wise person lives and works. He says a person who is content with whatever comes unasked, who does not envy others, and who remains the same in success and failure, is not bound by their actions even while they are working. The idea is that freedom comes from accepting what arrives without craving more and by letting go of the need to compare your results with someone else's.
verse.for_you: You are raising your children and watching them grow, and you are comparing your own path to the lives you see around you. The restlessness you feel comes from wanting the outcome to look a certain way before you allow yourself to rest.
verse.try_today: Notice one moment where you are comparing your children's path to someone else's.

verse.ref: Mahabharata · Vana Parva · Vana: Draupadi and Yudhishthira
verse.speaker: Draupadi
verse.setting: Draupadi describes a farmer who ploughs and sows, then waits for rain.
verse.sanskrit: वृष्टिश्चेन्नानुगृह्णीयादनेनास्तत्र कर्षकः / यदन्यः पुरुषः कुर्यात्तत्कृतं सफलं मया तच्चेदं फलमस्माकमपराधो न मे क्वचित् / इति धीरोऽन्ववेक्ष्यैव नात्मानं तत्रगर्हयेत्
verse.line: You ploughed and sowed. If the rain didn't come, that isn't your failure. Don't condemn yourself.
verse.translation: If the rain does not favour him, the farmer is not to blame. He tells himself: 'Whatever anyone could have done, I have done.' If the result is still this, the fault is not mine. Seeing this, the wise do not condemn themselves.
verse.why: Do right for its own sake, then work as if it all depends on you.

matched.label: I'm anxious about how things will turn out

prasang.title: Do right without reward, and keep working
prasang.summary: Draupadi questions a world where the good suffer; Yudhishthira answers that he does right because it is right, not for reward. Draupadi replies that effort still matters: fate rewards no one who waits.
prasang.lesson: Do right for its own sake, then work as if it all depends on you.

verse.meaning: Draupadi is speaking to Yudhishthira in the forest. She tells him about a farmer who ploughs and sows his field, then waits for the rain. She says the farmer is not to blame if the rain does not come. He tells himself he did all that anyone could do. If the result is still bad, the fault is not his. The wise do not condemn themselves.
verse.for_you: You have done the sowing. The waiting is not a failure of yours. Your part is the work. The harvest is not the lock on your rest.
verse.try_today: Notice one task you finished and let it be enough.
verse.scene_line: You are the farmer who has ploughed and sown, and now the field waits.
asks: How do I stop the harvest from ruling my rest?
What is the work I have already done today?
Can the result be separate from my worth?

verse.speaker: Seer
verse.setting: Follows the call to enjoy by letting go: how to live and work.
verse.sanskrit: कुर्वन्नेवेह कर्माणि जिजीविषेच्छतꣳ समाः । एवं त्वयि नान्यथेतोऽस्ति न कर्म लिप्यते नरे ॥
verse.line: Do your work and wish to live a full hundred years. Done in this spirit, action does not cling.
verse.translation: Doing your work here, you may wish to live a hundred years. For you there is no other way than this: done in this spirit, action does not cling to a person.
verse.why: Hold what you have lightly, keep working, and see yourself in everyone.

prasang.title: The Isha: enjoy by letting go
prasang.summary: Eighteen verses that open by saying everything belongs to the divine, so we should enjoy it without grasping. They go on to say we should work a full life without being bound, and see ourselves in all beings.
prasang.lesson: Hold what you have lightly, keep working, and see yourself in everyone.

verse.meaning: The seer is speaking to you, the reader, about how to live and work. They say to do your work and wish to live a full hundred years. The point is that you could hold what you have lightly, keep working, and see yourself in everyone.
verse.for_you: You are raising your children and your mind is restless because you could see a certain result before you let yourself rest. You can still do the work of the day and wish for a full life without letting the outcome hold you tight.
verse.try_today: Do one small task with the thought that you will live a hundred years.
verse.scene_line: You are in your own field, sowing seeds for your children, and the rain is not in your hands.
asks: How do I wish for a hundred years without getting caught in the result?
How do I see myself in everyone while I am so anxious about my children?
How do I let go of the outcome and still do the work?

verse.speaker: Vasishtha
verse.setting: Vasishtha teaches the disheartened young Rama that effort, not fate, shapes his life.
verse.sanskrit: यथा यथा प्रयत्नः स्याद्भवेदाशु फलं तथा । इति पौरुषमेवास्ति दैवमस्तु तदेव च ॥
verse.line: Results follow effort. Call it fate if you like, but it is the same effort.
verse.translation: As the effort, so quickly comes the fruit. So there is only effort; if you want to call it fate, it is that same effort.
verse.why: Your past effort shaped today; today's effort shapes tomorrow. Don't grieve what was never in your hands.

prasang.title: Vasishtha on self-effort: fate is only your past effort
prasang.summary: Vasishtha's first teaching to Rama is a long case for self-effort. What people call fate is simply the fruit of their own past effort, and present effort can overcome it, as the stronger of two rams wins. He also says not to torment yourself over what was beyond your power, and to steer your habits gently, like raising a child.
prasang.lesson: Your past effort shaped today; today's effort shapes tomorrow. Don't grieve what was never in your hands.

verse.meaning: Vasishtha speaks to the young prince Rama after Rama has given up on ruling and on life itself. The prince feels that his past has ruined his future, and he wants to disappear into the forest. Vasishtha sits with him and says that what people call fate is only the fruit of their own past effort. The effort you made yesterday built the world you stand in today. The effort you make today will build the world you stand in tomorrow. You are not the victim of a cruel destiny.
verse.for_you: You are standing in the middle of your children's lives, looking back at your own choices and wondering if you ruined their future. The restlessness is the weight of thinking you could control the harvest.
verse.try_today: Do one small part of your day's work without asking how it will turn out.
verse.scene_line: You stand in your own field, having sown the seed, waiting for a harvest that is not entirely yours.
asks: What is one small act of effort I can do today?
How do I separate my effort from the result I want?
Can I accept that some things are beyond my control?

story.title: King Janaka overhears the sages and keeps ruling, with a free mind
story.story_hook: One spring morning, a king out for a walk overheard a song that he could not stop thinking about.
story.summary: Walking in his spring garden, King Janaka overhears hidden sages singing about the self. Shaken, he climbs to his palace roof and questions everything he has lived for. When his doorkeeper calls him to the day's work, he decides not to run away: he gets up and does his duties, but with a mind that no longer clutches.
story.lesson: You don't have to leave your life to change it. Do the day's work with a mind that doesn't clutch.

anchor.speaker: Janaka
anchor.setting: King Janaka, alone on his palace roof after overhearing wandering sages, rethinks his life.
anchor.sanskrit: संपदश्च विचित्रा यास्ताश्चेच्चित्तेन संमताः । तत्ता अपि महारम्भा हन्त मन्ये महापदः ॥ आपदोऽपि विचित्रा यास्ताश्चेन्मनसि संमताः । तत्ता अपि महारम्भा मन्ये मनसि संपदः ॥
anchor.line: Good fortune the mind clutches becomes trouble. Trouble the mind accepts becomes a kind of fortune.
anchor.translation: All those dazzling fortunes, if the mind clings to them, are really great calamities in grand disguise. And all those varied misfortunes, if the mind accepts them, are really fortunes.
anchor.why: You don't have to leave your life to change it. Do the day's work with a mind that doesn't clutch.
anchor.misuse: Accepting a hardship doesn't mean not fixing what can be fixed.

story.hook_title: King Janaka overheard a song in his garden that he couldn't stop thinking about
story.teaser: King Janaka overheard a song in his garden that he couldn't stop thinking about
story.for_you: You do not have to leave your children or your home to find peace. The mind can stay open even while you are doing the work. You can do the day's work without letting the outcome hold you hostage. This is a freedom that lives inside the doing.

How can I rest while the day is still open?
